lesson_title: Your Rover Is Twenty Minutes Behind
hook_text: Tell a rover on Mars to stop before a rock, and it will not even hear you for twenty minutes.
clip_script: Light is the fastest thing there is: three hundred thousand kilometres every second, more than seven times around the Earth in one tick of a clock. But space is so big that even light takes time. Moonlight takes about one second to reach you. Sunlight takes eight minutes. When Mars is on the far side of the Sun, a radio command takes more than twenty minutes to arrive, so rovers have to think for themselves. Astronomers turned this into a ruler. A light minute is eighteen million kilometres. A light hour is about a billion. And a light year, the distance light travels in a year, is nine and a half trillion kilometres. It is a distance, not a time. The nearest star after the Sun is four point two four light years away. And here is the twist: you always see the past. The Andromeda Galaxy you can spot on a dark night is the light that left it two and a half million years ago.
visual_style: A whiteboard Earth and Mars with a radio wave crawling between them and a clock ticking, then a ruler marked in light seconds, minutes, hours and years stretching to a star, then Andromeda with a label '2.5 million years ago'.
pacing: A relatable delay, a new ruler, then a mind-bending twist.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and calculate a light minute yourself.
